sourceLine: your MentraOS work and the questions developers ask before they build for smart glasses

cards.title: Why the App Runtime Moved to the Phone
cards.angle: Meta opened Ray-Ban Display to third-party apps in May 2026 but runs them on the phone, not the glasses. Mentra reached the same architecture from the open-source side, and its own account says latency and ownership forced the move.
cards.evidence: Your June 2026 roadmap post describes the glasses to phone to cloud relay to developer app path and puts a button response at hundreds of milliseconds even in a good case; Mentra 3.0 (August 2026) moved every miniapp onto the phone with local STT and TTS models for when the connection drops. That is your own measurement, not a benchmark, and the article should say so.

Meta Opens Ray-Ban Display Glasses to Third-Party Developers

cards.title: Streaming Heat Is the Real Battery Ceiling
cards.angle: Meta says third-party apps cannot run on its glasses because of compute, thermal and battery limits. Your build log is the only public account of what that limit looks like on a bench.
cards.evidence: Making Mentra Live (December 2025) names the original MTK6765, says high-quality streaming overheated it after 15-plus minutes, and describes the MTK8766 upgrade and separating the WiFi chip from the processor. The product page rates 40-plus minutes of livestreaming and 10-plus hours of mixed use, two different use profiles, and the piece is what you changed in the board and video pipeline between them.

sources.title: New Meta Developer Tool Enables Third-parties to Bring Apps to its Smart Glasses

cards.title: One Vendor Ships Two Thirds of XR Devices
cards.angle: IDC put Meta at 68.7 percent of Q2 2026 shipments across its combined XR headset and glasses tracker, and Meta's developer program is a preview with no stated review process. An open OS is only an argument if it runs on hardware people can buy.
cards.evidence: MentraOS is Apache 2.0, supports Mentra Live, Even Realities G1 and G2 and Vuzix Z100, and your first 1,000-unit batch sold out in under a month. Your August post makes the open-platform case in general terms; the specific piece is what an open runtime lets an enterprise control across those devices.
